title: Futurism & The Aestheticization of Speed
subtitle: The Italian avant-garde movement celebrating machinery and kinetic energy
summary: Founded by F.T. Marinetti in 1909, Futurism embraced technology, dynamic movement, airplanes, and industrial power, rejecting historical academic tradition in favor of kinetic rhythm.
keyTakeaway: Futurism glorified the velocity and violent energy of modern industrial society.

title: Dadaism & Anti-Art Absurdity
subtitle: The radical international movement rejecting bourgeois art conventions
summary: Emerging during WWI, Dada artists like Marcel Duchamp used ready-mades, collage, and nonsensical poetry to protest the rationalist logic that led to mechanical warfare.
keyTakeaway: Dada used absurdity to dismantle conventional definitions of art and institutional power.

title: De Stijl & Neoplasticist Reduction
subtitle: Piet Mondrian and Theo van Doesburg's search for universal harmony
summary: De Stijl reduced art to pure abstraction using only primary colors (red, blue, yellow) alongside black, white, and non-colors constrained within orthogonal horizontal-vertical grids.
keyTakeaway: Neoplasticism sought absolute visual equilibrium through extreme geometric reduction.

title: Constructivism & Art for Social Utility
subtitle: Russian avant-garde movement integrating art directly into industrial life
summary: Constructivists rejected autonomous easel painting, advocating instead that artists become designers, engineers, and typographers producing functional objects for socialist society.
keyTakeaway: Art was stripped of bourgeois decoration to become a direct tool for social transformation.

summary: Tenebrism (developed by Caravaggio) uses stark spotlighting emerging from pitch-black backgrounds, creating intense psychological drama and spatial depth in oil paintings.
keyTakeaway: Extreme tonal contrast transforms light into a physical dramatic actor on canvas.

title: Sfumato & Soft Atmospheric Transition
subtitle: Leonardo da Vinci's technique of blending colors without perceptive lines
summary: Sfumato (from Italian 'evaporated like smoke') applies ultra-thin translucent glazes to blur sharp contours, achieving soft atmospheric transitions seen in the Mona Lisa's smile.
keyTakeaway: Gradual tonal blending mirrors natural atmospheric optics, eliminating artificial hard outlines.

title: Encaustic Painting & Hot Wax Pigments
subtitle: Ancient technique fusing colored beeswax onto wooden panels
summary: Practiced in Fayum mummy portraits, encaustic painting mixes molten beeswax with mineral pigments, producing luminous, highly durable surfaces that resist moisture for millennia.
keyTakeaway: Molten beeswax creates deep translucent jewel-toned layers that preserve color vibrance across centuries.

title: Pointillism & Chromoluminarism
subtitle: Seurat's optical color mixing via tiny distinct dots of pure pigment
summary: Georges Seurat applied small dots of pure unmixed color side-by-side on canvas, relying on the viewer's eye to optically blend the colors into vibrant glowing hues.
keyTakeaway: Color perception occurs inside the viewer's eye through optical synthesis rather than pallet mixing.

title: Trompe-l'œil & Hyper-Realistic Illusion
subtitle: Architectural and canvas painting techniques designed to trick the eye
summary: Trompe-l'œil ('deceive the eye') uses precise perspective, realistic shadows, and shallow depth of field to convince viewers that 2D painted objects exist in physical 3D space.
keyTakeaway: Painting simulates physical reality so convincingly that visual perception temporarily suspended belief.

title: Sfumato & Soft Atmospheric Transition
subtitle: Leonardo da Vinci's technique of blending colors without perceptive lines
summary: Sfumato (from Italian 'evaporated like smoke') applies ultra-thin translucent glazes to blur sharp contours, achieving soft atmospheric transitions seen in the Mona Lisa's smile.
keyTakeaway: Gradual tonal blending mirrors natural atmospheric optics, eliminating artificial hard outlines.

title: Encaustic Painting & Hot Wax Pigments
subtitle: Ancient technique fusing colored beeswax onto wooden panels
summary: Practiced in Fayum mummy portraits, encaustic painting mixes molten beeswax with mineral pigments, producing luminous, highly durable surfaces that resist moisture for millennia.
keyTakeaway: Molten beeswax creates deep translucent jewel-toned layers that preserve color vibrance across centuries.

title: Pointillism & Chromoluminarism
subtitle: Seurat's optical color mixing via tiny distinct dots of pure pigment
summary: Georges Seurat applied small dots of pure unmixed color side-by-side on canvas, relying on the viewer's eye to optically blend the colors into vibrant glowing hues.
keyTakeaway: Color perception occurs inside the viewer's eye through optical synthesis rather than pallet mixing.

title: Trompe-l'œil & Hyper-Realistic Illusion
subtitle: Architectural and canvas painting techniques designed to trick the eye
summary: Trompe-l'œil ('deceive the eye') uses precise perspective, realistic shadows, and shallow depth of field to convince viewers that 2D painted objects exist in physical 3D space.
keyTakeaway: Painting simulates physical reality so convincingly that visual perception temporarily suspended belief.

title: Moral Licensing & Self-Regulating Virtue
subtitle: The psychological phenomenon where past good deeds excuse subsequent bad behavior

summary: In economics and ethics, moral hazard arises when one party takes risks because the financial or social burdens of failure fall entirely on another party (e.g. government bank bailouts).
keyTakeaway: Insulating decision-makers from consequences inevitably leads to unethical and reckless behavior.

summary: Studies show people often experience strong gut feelings that an action is morally wrong, yet remain unable to produce any logical rationale when pressed—a state called moral dumbfounding.
keyTakeaway: Moral judgment is driven by immediate emotional gut reactions, with reasoning acting as an post-hoc advocate.

summary: Evolutionary biology explains altruism through Hamilton's Rule (rb > c), showing that individuals sacrifice for relatives to ensure shared genetic representation in future generations.

summary: Moral luck occurs when an agent is held morally accountable for an outcome determined largely by luck—such as two drunk drivers, one of whom hits a pedestrian while the other gets home safely.
keyTakeaway: We praise or blame people for outcomes shaped by forces entirely beyond their control.

subtitle: How insulation from risk encourages reckless moral decision making
summary: In economics and ethics, moral hazard arises when one party takes risks because the financial or social burdens of failure fall entirely on another party (e.g. government bank bailouts).
keyTakeaway: Insulating decision-makers from consequences inevitably leads to unethical and reckless behavior.
